title: 01. Fundamentals: String Indexing & Slicing
summary: Indexing and slicing are how you extract parts of a string. This is one of the most-used features in Python.

sections.title: CONCEPT EXPLANATION
sections.body:
Indexing and slicing are how you **extract parts of a string**. This is one of the most-used features in Python.

### Indexing — Access a Single Character:
```
String:   P  y  t  h  o  n
Index:    0  1  2  3  4  5    ← Positive indices (left to right)
          -6 -5 -4 -3 -2 -1  ← Negative indices (right to left)
```

### Slicing — Extract a Substring:
```python
s[start:stop:step]
# start → where to BEGIN (inclusive)
# stop  → where to END (exclusive — NOT included!)
# step  → how many positions to jump (default=1)
```

### ⚠️ Critical Rules:
- Indices start at **0** (not 1!)
- `stop` is **exclusive** — `s[0:3]` gives characters at index 0, 1, 2 (NOT 3)
- Negative indices count from the **end**: `-1` = last character
- Out-of-range index in `[]` → `IndexError`
- Out-of-range in slicing → **no error** (Python clips gracefully!)

sections.title: 5 EXAMPLES
sections.body:
### Example 1: Basic Indexing
```python
text = "Python Programming"
#       0123456789...

# Positive indexing (left to right)
print(text[0])      # P — first character
print(text[1])      # y
print(text[6])      # (space)
print(text[7])      # P

# Negative indexing (right to left)
print(text[-1])     # g — last character
print(text[-2])     # n
print(text[-11])    # P

# Length and last valid index
print(len(text))    # 18
# Valid indices: 0 to 17, or -1 to -18

# ❌ Out of range
try:
    print(text[100])
except IndexError as e:
    print(f"Error: {e}")  # string index out of range

# ✅ Out of range in SLICE — no error!
print(text[0:100])   # "Python Programming" — clips to end
print(text[100:])    # "" — empty string
```

### Example 2: Basic Slicing — Start, Stop, Step
```python
text = "Hello, World!"
#       0123456789012

# Basic slices [start:stop]
print(text[0:5])     # Hello  (index 0,1,2,3,4)
print(text[7:12])    # World
print(text[0:7])     # Hello,

# Omitting start (defaults to 0)
print(text[:5])      # Hello

# Omitting stop (defaults to end)
print(text[7:])      # World!

# Omitting both (copy entire string)
print(text[:])       # Hello, World!

# Negative indices in slices
print(text[-6:])     # World!    (last 6 characters)
print(text[:-7])     # Hello,    (everything except last 7)
print(text[-6:-1])   # World     (skip last char)

# Step parameter
print(text[::2])     # Hlo ol!  (every 2nd char)
print(text[::3])     # H,Wr     (every 3rd char)
```

### Example 3: Reverse, Step, and Advanced Slicing
```python
text = "Python"

# Reverse a string — the famous trick!
reversed_text = text[::-1]
print(reversed_text)    # nohtyP

# Step = 2 (every other character)
print(text[::2])        # Pto
print(text[1::2])       # yhn  (start from index 1)

# Negative step — go backwards
print(text[5:1:-1])     # nthy  (from index 5 down to 2)
print(text[::-2])       # nhy   (every 2nd char, backwards)

# Practical: check if a word is a palindrome
def is_palindrome(word):
    word = word.lower()
    return word == word[::-1]

words = ["racecar", "hello", "madam", "Python", "level"]
for w in words:
    print(f"  '{w}': {'✅ Palindrome' if is_palindrome(w) else '❌ Not palindrome'}")

# Extract domain from email
email = "veerababu@example.com"
at_index = email.index("@")
username = email[:at_index]
domain   = email[at_index+1:]
print(f"Username: {username}, Domain: {domain}")
```

### Example 4: Real-World Slicing Patterns
```python
# Pattern 1: Extract date components from ISO format
date_str = "2026-05-02"
year  = date_str[:4]      # "2026"
month = date_str[5:7]     # "05"
day   = date_str[8:10]    # "02"
print(f"Year: {year}, Month: {month}, Day: {day}")

# Pattern 2: Credit card masking
card_number = "4532111122223333"
masked = "*" * 12 + card_number[-4:]
print(f"Card: {masked}")   # ************3333

# Pattern 3: File extension extraction
filename = "report_2026.pdf"
# Find last dot
last_dot  = filename.rfind(".")
name_part = filename[:last_dot]
extension = filename[last_dot+1:]
print(f"Name: {name_part}, Extension: {extension}")

# Pattern 4: Truncate long strings with ellipsis
def truncate(text, max_length=50):
    if len(text) <= max_length:
        return text
    return text[:max_length-3] + "..."

long_text = "This is a very long product description that needs to be truncated"
print(truncate(long_text, 30))  # "This is a very long product..."

# Pattern 5: Log prefix extraction
log = "2026-05-02 10:30:45 [ERROR] Database connection failed"
timestamp = log[:19]        # "2026-05-02 10:30:45"
level     = log[21:26]      # "[ERRO"... better use split
print(f"Timestamp: {timestamp}")
```

### Example 5: Slicing with Variables and Dynamic Indices
```python
# Finding and slicing based on character positions
url = "https://www.example.com/products/laptop?id=123&color=red"

# Extract different parts dynamically
protocol_end = url.index("://")
protocol     = url[:protocol_end]          # "https"

domain_start = protocol_end + 3
domain_end   = url.index("/", domain_start)
domain       = url[domain_start:domain_end]  # "www.example.com"

path_end = url.index("?") if "?" in url else len(url)
path     = url[domain_end:path_end]          # "/products/laptop"

query = url[path_end+1:] if "?" in url else ""  # "id=123&color=red"

print(f"Protocol: {protocol}")
print(f"Domain:   {domain}")
print(f"Path:     {path}")
print(f"Query:    {query}")

# Sliding window over a string
text  = "abcdefghij"
width = 3
print(f"\nSliding window (width={width}):")
for i in range(len(text) - width + 1):
    window = text[i:i+width]
    print(f"  [{i}:{i+width}] = '{window}'")
```

quiz.question: Why is the stop index in Python slicing exclusive?
options: Both convert strings to lowercase, but casefold() is more aggressive and designed specifically for caseless string matching (Unicode-aware case-insensitive comparison).…
isspace() returns True if ALL characters are whitespace AND the string is non-empty.
No — strings are immutable in Python. strip() (and all string methods) always return a NEW string object.
Python's slicing convention [start:stop] makes stop exclusive for mathematical elegance and practical convenience: > 1. len(s[a:b]) == b - a — length is simply stop…
quiz.explanation: Python's slicing convention [start:stop] makes stop exclusive for mathematical elegance and practical convenience: len(s[a:b]) == b - a — length is simply stop minus start s[:n] + s[n:] always equals s — clean splitting at any index s[0:n] gives exactly n characters — intuitive count Compare: if stop were inclusive, s[0:0] would give one character (weird!), and length calculation would be b - a + 1.

quiz.question: What is the difference between s[-1] and s[len(s)-1]?
options: 5-Year Experience Answer: > "Python 3 strings are Unicode by default — they can store any character from any language.
In a raw string, backslashes are treated as literal backslash characters — they don't act as escape sequence prefixes.
There's no built-in findnth() in Python, but it's easy to implement: > > > Alternative using split(): > > > In production I use the loop version — it's O(n·m) where n is…
They produce the same result — both access the last character.
quiz.explanation: They produce the same result — both access the last character. But negative indexing is: More readable: s[-1] is instantly recognizable as 'last character' Safer for empty strings: well, both crash on empty string with IndexError Works in slices: s[-3:] cleanly means 'last 3 characters' — try writing that with len() — it's s[len(s)-3:], much clunkier Python calculates s[-n] as s[len(s)-n] internally.

quiz.question: What does s[:] do and why is it useful?
options: The start and end parameters define a search window within the string.
zfill() is smart about signs — it inserts zeros AFTER the sign character: > > > Practical uses in production: > - Invoice numbers: str(invoice_id).zfill(8) → '00000042'…
All three check if a string represents a number, but they differ in what they accept: > > - isdecimal() — strictest: only 0-9 ASCII decimal digits.
s[:] with both start and stop omitted returns a shallow copy of the string.
quiz.explanation: s[:] with both start and stop omitted returns a shallow copy of the string. Since strings are immutable in Python, copying a string doesn't provide the usual 'independent mutable copy' benefit that list[:] gives.

quiz.question: What happens when slice indices are out of range?
options: Three ways, in order of Pythonicity: > > Performance: [::-1] is fastest — implemented in C, single pass. ''.join(reversed(s)) is also fast.
I use a systematic approach for string performance: > > Step 1: Profile to find the bottleneck > > > Step 2: Common optimizations in order of impact: > > > Step 3:…
5-Year Experience Answer: > "String interning is Python's optimization where it reuses the same memory object for identical string literals instead of creating duplicate…
Slicing is forgiving — Python clips out-of-range indices to valid boundaries: > > This is opposite to direct indexing (s[100] raises IndexError).
quiz.explanation: Slicing is forgiving — Python clips out-of-range indices to valid boundaries: This is opposite to direct indexing (s[100] raises IndexError). The design rationale: indexing fetches a specific position (invalid position = error), while slicing defines a range (invalid range = empty range, not an error).

options: 5-Year Experience Answer: > "Python 3 strings are Unicode by default — they can store any character from any language.
All three try to match a pattern against a string but differ in WHERE they look: > > - re.match(): Only matches at the very beginning of the string. re.match(r'\\d+',…
Both convert to bytes but with different use cases: > > > > The dangerous pitfall: bytes(5) gives 5 zero bytes, NOT the text '5'!
Three ways, in order of Pythonicity: > > Performance: [::-1] is fastest — implemented in C, single pass. ''.join(reversed(s)) is also fast.
quiz.explanation: Three ways, in order of Pythonicity: Performance: [::-1] is fastest — implemented in C, single pass. ''.join(reversed(s)) is also fast. The loop is O(n²) due to string immutability. Interview bonus: Unicode reversal is tricky with combining characters: In production, I use [::-1] for ASCII, and have a utility function for Unicode-safe reversal when dealing with international user input." ---
